newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World trade body faces key week, major disputes.
newsitem.headline: World trade body faces key week, major disputes.

text.p: The World Trade Organisation pushes this week into some of the most controversial and potentially explosive issues on its agenda as it prepares for its first ministerial conference in December.

Trade rows between the major powers that could test their commitment to the WTO system and stark disagreements between developed and developing countries over textiles and treatment of direct investment are the major themes.

The 21-month-old body's General Council will on Monday also be seeking to refine the programme for the December meeting in Singapore -- a debate reflecting strong differences over the direction the WTO should take up to the end of the century.

And a working party will look later in the week into the application for membership from one of the two major economies still outside the WTO, Russia, while preparing for new talks on the accession of the other, China, at the end of the month.

"We are certainly getting to some of the crunch issues, and although there will be no major decisions this will be a week that may one day be seen as a time of definition for the WTO," said one Geneva trade envoy.

Centrepiece will be a meeting on Wednesday of the Dispute Settlement Body (DSB), widely viewed as the one real success story since the WTO replaced the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) on January 1 1995.

The DSB, under the streamlined procedure that replaced the plodding GATT process, will set up panels in two major cases brought by the United States -- against Japan over photofilm and against the European Union over hormone-treated beef.

And in the first strongly political dispute to come before the body, the EU will request -- but almost certainly not get this time round -- a panel on whether the U.S. Helms-Burton law, aimed at limiting investment in Cuba, violates WTO rules.
The three cases reflect long-standing tensions between the trio and contain the seeds of serious confrontation that could tear at the carefully-woven fabric of the WTO.

U.S. officials make clear they see the photo-film challenge -- widely known as the Kodak-Fuji case -- as a test of whether the trade body can attack what Washington says is a network of hidden barriers used by Japan against all foreign goods.

In the hormone case, the EU will be defending a 10-year ban on imports of meat from cattle treated with growth stimulants -- an issue where Brussels is under strong pressure from European consumers not to give way.

In the Helms-Burton case, in which the EU is formally backed by Canada and informally by almost every other country in the 124-member WTO, the right of a state to legislate to limit another's trade contacts with a third will be tested.
U.S. officials argue the law is covered by a GATT clause allowing countries to suspend trade agreements if they deem their national security is threatened.

Although the process can take up to 18 months before a final ruling, a panel finding against the U.S. would certainly reinforce opponents of the WTO in Washington. But a finding for, diplomats fear, would open the way to widespread abuse of the clause.
On Tuesday, the WTO Goods Council will hear further complaints from Asian countries that the big powers are not moving fast enough under the 1994 world trade treaty to open up their textile markets.

And on Wednesday the WTO secretariat issues a report that Director-General Renato Ruggiero says will make a "compelling case" for agreement at Singapore to start discussion of a possible accord on global free trade rules on investment.

The report, unusually trenchant, is likely to anger many emerging economies such as India and Malaysia who fear such rules will limit their powers to nurture national business and keep powerful transnational corporations in check. REUTER 130937 GMT oct 96
